item.title: A Shooting at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto Exposes a Neighborhood’s Guns-for-Hire Network
item.description: A shooting at a U.S. Consulate has thrust a neighborhood with a troubled past into the center of an emerging criminal phenomenon: young guns for hire as gig workers in the underworld economy.
item.dc:creator: Vjosa Isai and Ian Willms
item.media:credit: Ian Willms for The New York Times
item.media:description: Outside 15 Martha Eaton Way in Toronto.

item.title: Trump’s Other Hold on the Americas: The Visa
item.description: As part of its expansionist approach to the Western Hemisphere, the Trump administration is trying to reassert its dominance, one U.S. visa at a time.
item.dc:creator: Emiliano Rodríguez Mega, Emma Bubola, Gabriel Labrador and David Bolaños
item.media:credit: Kenny Holston/The New York Times
item.media:description: The State Department overseen by Marco Rubio has restored the visas of political figures in Central America once penalized by the U.S. government and has revoked visas for others.

item.title: Summer Camps Strive to Stay Part of Canadian Life, Despite Hurdles
item.description: Long a tradition for many kids and teenagers across the country, overnight camps are facing financial and cultural hurdles as inflation bites and parenting trends shift.
item.dc:creator: Matina Stevis-Gridneff

item.title: Canadian Petition to Expel U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra Takes Off
item.description: Mr. Hoekstra has been President Trump’s faithful messenger in Canada amid a historic low in relations. More than 200,000 Canadians want him gone.
item.dc:creator: Matina Stevis-Gridneff
item.media:credit: Ian Austen/The New York Times
item.media:description: Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, at the embassy’s July 4 party at his official residence in Ottawa.

item.title: How Cyclospora Evaded the U.S. Food Safety System to Sicken Thousands
item.description: The Trump administration delayed a rule last year that could have sped up the effort to pinpoint the source of the contamination. Critics charge that food safety oversight has eroded overall.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett and Julie Creswell
item.media:credit: Al Drago for The New York Times
item.media:description: Last year the Food and Drug Administration cut a program that tracked cyclospora outbreaks and delayed a rule that would have required companies to swiftly provide supply chain records in investigations of foodborne disease outbreaks.

item.title: A Prominent Mexican Politician Says U.S. Revoked His Visa
item.description: Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, a former president’s son, lashed out at the Trump administration after he said it canceled his visa, another flashpoint in the tense U.S.-Mexico relationship.
item.dc:creator: Jack Nicas, Annie Correal and Emiliano Rodríguez Mega
item.media:credit: Henry Romero/Reuters
item.media:description: Andrés Manuel López Beltrán is the son of Mexico’s former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who is still a key leader of Morena, Mexico’s dominant political party.

item.title: 8 Matisse Works, Looted from Library in Brazil, Are Recovered
item.description: The prints by the French master were taken in São Paulo last year in a brazen daylight heist.
item.dc:creator: John Yoon
item.media:credit: São Paulo Police Press Office, via Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: A handout photo released by the São Paulo police press office showing the recovered Matisse works.

item.title: After 2 Plasma Donor Deaths, Company Pauses Clinics in Canada
item.description: Grifols, a Spanish company, said “unfounded attention” on its blood plasma business in Canada had led it to temporarily end collections at 17 clinics.
item.dc:creator: Vjosa Isai
item.media:credit: Enric Fontcuberta/EPA, via Shutterstock
item.media:description: Donating plasma for Grifols at a hospital in Barcelona in 2020. The company has suspended collecting plasma in Canada because of scrutiny over two deaths.

item.title: Topos Azteca, a Mexican Volunteer Rescue Group, Helps With Rescue Efforts After Colombia Earthquake
item.description: Topos Azteca, a Mexican volunteer rescue group that works worldwide and helped after the Sept. 11 attacks, arrived in Colombia after searching for survivors in Venezuela.
item.dc:creator: Genevieve Glatsky and Federico Rios
item.media:credit: Federico Rios for The New York Times
item.media:description: A member of Topos Azteca working among the rubble on Wednesday in Cali, Colombia.

item.title: Brazil’s Disease-Fighting Mosquitoes
item.description: Our reporter, Apoorva Mandavilli, goes inside a mosquito factory in Brazil, where scientists are producing millions of mosquitoes to fight deadly tropical diseases in a warming world.
item.dc:creator: Apoorva Mandavilli, Leila Medina, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Joey Sendaydiego and Tuna Mayer

item.title: A City Mobilizes Against a Stubborn Health Threat: Mosquitoes
item.description: The city of Belém in northern Brazil was overwhelmed by an outbreak of dengue two years ago. An all-out municipal effort has reduced cases and may offer lessons to American cities.
item.dc:creator: Apoorva Mandavilli and Alessandro Falco
item.media:description: A health worker discarding water from a larvicide dissemination unit in Belém, Brazil, last month.

item.title: Come for the Cottage in ‘Heated Rivalry.’ Stay for Everything Else.
item.description: The chance to see the hideaway from the hit queer hockey romance lured me to Canada’s cottage country. But it was the glistening lakes and weep-worthy sunsets that won me over.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Bahr and Brendan George Ko
item.media:description: One of the many attractions in the Muskoka region of Ontario: the free Tuesday-evening water-skiing show on Lake Muskoka in Bala.

item.title: Ecuadorean Fishing Boats Hit by Mystery Attackers
item.description: Ecuadorean crews plying the waters of the Pacific have been targeted by a mysterious outfit equipped with drones. Some sailors appear to have lost their lives.

item.title: Trump Tariffs Force Some Canadian Companies to Move South of the Border
item.description: If President Trump moves ahead with 50 percent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian products later this month, some companies may only survive by relocating to the United States.
item.dc:creator: Ian Austen
item.media:credit: Ian Austen/The New York Times
item.media:description: Turning nearly pure copper into electrical wires is one of the first stages of production at Northern Cables in Brockville, Ontario.

item.title: A Rescue Effort After Colombia’s Earthquake
item.description: Our reporter Genevieve Glatsky, who is based in Colombia, witnesses the rescue of a buried earthquake survivor in the city of Cali.

item.title: Searching for Survivors After Colombia’s Earthquake

item.title: Before Trump’s Catering Container Ruse, Other Presidents Obscured Risky Travel Plans

item.title: As Death Toll From Colombia Earthquake Rises to at Least 181, Rescuers Hunt for Survivors
item.description: “We heard them screaming,” said one rescuer in Cali, where emergency workers and volunteers are racing against time to find the living trapped in the rubble.

item.title: What to Know About the Cuban Mafia in Quintana Roo
item.description: A group of Cuban men in Mexico was charged with smuggling people to the United States. One of its leaders said Raúl Castro’s grandson helped, according to interviews and court records.

item.media:credit: Jae C. Hong/Associated Press
item.media:description: The former Los Angeles Dodgers player Yasiel Puig was one of the Cubans smuggled into the United States by a criminal group known as the Cuban Mafia.

item.title: How Raúl Castro’s Grandson, Raúl G. Rodríguez Castro, Became a Power Broker

item.media:description: A rescue dog and his guide are among those looking for survivors on Monday in Cali, Colombia.

item.title: Here Is Where Colombia’s Quake Hit Hardest

item.title: Colombia Quake Chases Teenage Venezuelan Brothers From Their New Home
item.description: A pair of brothers who lost their mother and other family members in Venezuela and were profiled by The New York Times have now survived deadly quakes in two countries.
item.dc:creator: Julie Turkewitz
item.media:credit: Adriana Loureiro Fernandez for The New York Times
item.media:description: Deivid Delfín, 44, with his two surviving sons, Winder, 17, left, and Deivi, 15, right, in Venezuela in June, after twin earthquakes killed the boys’ mother, younger brother and grandmother.
